speaker: maya
text: Last time: mercantilism, the Navigation Acts, and salutary neglect. London's money theory, and the loopholes the colonies grew rich in. As promised: a young English preacher named Whitefield, an open field, and crowds that came to weep. Four boxes this time: Whitefield, Edwards, Franklin's counterweight, and the splits the revival left behind. Circle the ones you couldn't explain. Twelve minutes, starting now.

speaker: marcus
text: Before the fire, the tinder. By the 1730s, plenty of colonial churches had gone cold. Formal, established, ministers reading their sermons and sitting down. Membership was slipping, and the zeal with it.

speaker: maya
text: So what do you do when the pews start emptying?

speaker: marcus
text: New England tried a compromise back in 1662. The Half-Way Covenant: if you couldn't prove you'd been converted, you could still be baptized and join as a partial member. You got the pews, but voting and communion stayed off-limits.

speaker: maya
text: Full pews, thinner commitment.

speaker: marcus
text: That was the trade. And a generation was hungry for religion that did something to them. Then the spark: preachers traveling town to town, preaching outdoors, because no building could hold the crowds.

speaker: maya
text: I went to an outdoor concert in Phoenix one July. Twenty thousand people, no shade, everyone melting by the second song. Standing through a two-hour sermon in that? Respect.

speaker: marcus
text: In 1739, a young Englishman in his mid-twenties named George Whitefield crossed the Atlantic and started preaching in open fields. Crowds in the thousands, and by the newspapers' counts, twenty-five thousand in a field.

speaker: maya
text: No speakers, twenty-five thousand people. How did the back rows hear him?

speaker: marcus
text: His voice just carried. Benjamin Franklin once stood at the back of a Philadelphia crowd and walked backward down Market Street until the voice blurred. Then he did the math: a semicircle of listeners at that distance, two square feet each, and he computed Whitefield could be heard by more than thirty thousand.

speaker: maya
text: Ben Franklin did a sound check. In the 1740s.

speaker: marcus
text: He did. And Franklin's press printed the sermons, so the voice traveled farther than the man. Franklin's press and Whitefield's fame fed each other. The sermons sold newspapers; the newspapers spread the name. Historians call Whitefield America's first celebrity.

speaker: maya
text: Was he really the first? Nobody was famous before him?

speaker: marcus
text: He's called the first because the fame crossed the ocean on paper. The newspapers carried him the way the ships carried everything else.

speaker: maya
text: Exam tip: when a stimulus describes open-air crowds and weeping, name the method behind it. Emotional preaching against the old establishment.

speaker: marcus
text: And the funny true detail: Franklin thought Whitefield's orphanage should be built in Philadelphia, not Georgia. He went to a sermon meaning to give nothing. By the end he'd emptied his whole pocket into the collection dish, gold and all.

speaker: maya
text: The skeptic never converted — but he did empty his whole pocket.

speaker: marcus
text: Common mistake for box one: don't write that Whitefield started the revival. The fire was already smoldering in the 1730s. He poured the gasoline.

speaker: maya
text: Your turn. You're a church elder in 1662. Membership is falling because the conversion test is too hard. Your deacons want the halfway rule. What are you risking?

speaker: maya
text: Full pews, thinner faith. Checking that one. Whitefield, box one.

speaker: marcus
text: Now the other preacher. And he's nothing like Whitefield.

speaker: maya
text: So Edwards is the loud one, the weeper, acting out his sermons?

speaker: marcus
text: Backwards. That's Whitefield: the weeping, the acting, the crowds. Edwards barely raised his voice. His weapon was the argument.

speaker: maya
text: The easy flip to avoid. Edwards argued, Whitefield acted.

speaker: marcus
text: Jonathan Edwards, a Massachusetts theologian, deep and careful. On July 8, 1741, in Enfield, Connecticut, he preached what's often called the most famous sermon in American history: "Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God."

speaker: maya
text: "The God that holds you over the pit of hell, much as one holds a spider, or some loathsome insect, over the fire."

speaker: marcus
text: His actual words. And the famous account says he didn't shout it. He read it, nearly flat, barely looking up, while the congregation came apart around him.

speaker: maya
text: That's scarier, honestly. The calm ones are always scarier.

speaker: marcus
text: They used different weapons to make the same break with the old churches. Whitefield took religion to the fields; Edwards argued you into terror. Both cut out the middleman and put the conversion on the individual.

speaker: maya
text: Someone on TikTok does the Enfield sermon as ASMR. The flat voice, the screaming congregation. Two million likes.

speaker: marcus
text: Of course that's a thing. But the delivery is the point: feeling was the message. And the message many hearers took was that anyone could be saved, a choice away from the old ideas of predestination.

speaker: maya
text: Exam tip: if the test hands you the spider line, they're testing style, not theology. Feeling against the formal churches.

speaker: marcus
text: And the revival had casualties. Edwards tightened the rules on who could take communion, and in 1750 his own congregation at Northampton voted him out. The most famous theologian in the colonies, dismissed by his own church.

speaker: maya
text: Edwards was the opposite of a showman — all argument, no theater — and his own congregation fired him anyway.

speaker: marcus
text: Easy mix-up on box two: don't picture Edwards shouting. The calm delivery is the point — the famous account has him reading the sermon nearly flat, barely looking up, and that stillness is what made it terrifying.

speaker: marcus
text: Franklin was watching all of this, and he offered a different answer entirely. Box three: the counterweight.

speaker: maya
text: "Early to bed, early to rise" guy. I didn't know that was a whole worldview.

speaker: marcus
text: It was. From 1732, for twenty-five years, Franklin published Poor Richard's Almanack: weather, household tips, and aphorisms about work and thrift. "A penny saved is a penny earned." The jokes carried the Enlightenment: reason over revelation, the self-made man as a project.

speaker: maya
text: And the Junto?

speaker: marcus
text: In 1727 he started the Junto, a club of tradesmen who met to argue morals and politics and pooled their books until they'd built a lending library — the Enlightenment as a social club. Then the electricity work: the lightning rod, and a reputation that reached across the Atlantic.

speaker: maya
text: The kite. Did he actually fly it in a thunderstorm?

speaker: marcus
text: The famous story is shakier than the textbooks let on. Whether Franklin himself ever stood in a storm holding that string, nobody's fully sure. But the experiments were real, and they made him famous across the Atlantic before he was a revolutionary.

speaker: maya
text: So the Awakening crowds are out in the fields weeping, and the Junto guys are indoors going, "Actually, let's reason about this."

speaker: marcus
text: Feeling against reason — that's the split in one line. And the key term is deism: the idea that God wound up the universe like a clock and stepped back. No miracles in the daily weather. If you want to know how the world works, use your reason.

speaker: maya
text: Common mistake for box three: don't file Franklin under the Awakening. His press carried the revival, but his mind was on the Enlightenment.

speaker: marcus
text: Exam tip: when Franklin shows up on a question, the answer is almost always the Enlightenment. The revival is the wrong column.

speaker: maya
text: While the crowds were weeping in the fields, Franklin was indoors reasoning.

speaker: marcus
text: Then the aftershock. The revival's fans became the New Lights. The old guard, the Old Lights.

speaker: maya
text: Your turn. Your church just split over the revival. Half the members walk out to start their own congregation. They've never run anything before. What do they have to learn, fast?

speaker: maya
text: How to organize. Raise money, pick leaders, argue in public, defy the established church and survive it.

speaker: marcus
text: That organizing is the aftershock. Ordinary colonists practiced standing up to authority, and they watched it work. New denominations grew out of the fire: Baptists, Methodists. The revival even founded colleges. Princeton was chartered in 1746 by New Light Presbyterians.

speaker: maya
text: Exam tip: New Light versus Old Light questions hinge on authority. Who gets to decide what counts as real religion?

speaker: marcus
text: And here's the debate historians still have. Some call the Awakening the first thing all the colonies ever experienced together. The same sermons, the same crowds, from New England down to Georgia.

speaker: maya
text: And some don't buy that.

speaker: marcus
text: Others say it's overstated. The revivals never touched half the colonies, and in some places the fire burned out fast. So the big question: did the Awakening help cause the Revolution?

speaker: maya
text: Give me both sides.

speaker: marcus
text: The case for: it trained colonists to defy authority, and gave them a shared experience. A rehearsal, some historians say, for 1776. The case against: the fires died down decades before the war, plenty of patriot leaders were never awakened, and both movements may just come from the same restless individualism. I don't think that's settled.

speaker: maya
text: So the answer is "argue both sides." Very AP of them.

speaker: marcus
text: About as AP as it gets.

speaker: maya
text: Common mistake for box four: the trap answer is "the Awakening caused the Revolution." It's a live debate, not a fact.

speaker: maya
text: No goodbyes yet.

speaker: maya
text: Four boxes, let's land them. One: Whitefield. Cold churches, the 1662 halfway compromise, and a twenty-something Englishman preaching to fields in 1739. The sound check said thirty thousand could hear him. Two: Edwards. Enfield, July 1741, the spider over the fire, read nearly flat. The argument got him fired in 1750. Three: Franklin's counterweight. The Almanack from 1732, the Junto in 1727, the clockmaker God, reason answering feeling. Four: the splits. The Old Lights were the revival fans, the New Lights held the line, and the organizing taught colonists to defy authority.

speaker: marcus
text: One correction.

speaker: maya
text: Which did I flip?

speaker: marcus
text: The lights. The New Lights were the revival fans. The Old Lights held the line.

speaker: maya
text: I did flip it. New Lights, the revival. Old Lights, the old guard. Landing all four.

speaker: maya
text: Three questions, AP-shaped. Say your answer before I give it.

speaker: maya
text: One. The stimulus is Edwards, 1741, and these are his actual words: "The God that holds you over the pit of hell, much as one holds a spider, or some loathsome insect, over the fire." Who's preaching, and what's the point of this passage?

speaker: maya
text: Jonathan Edwards, at Enfield, Connecticut, in July 1741 — the spider image, the pit of hell, the famous sermon title. The point is the method, not the theology: terror as conversion, the Awakening's emotional style doing what the cold, formal churches couldn't.

speaker: maya
text: Two. Why did the Awakening split churches into New Lights and Old Lights?

speaker: maya
text: The split was a fight over authority — itinerant preachers drew crowds without invitations, and converts claimed their own experience outranked the old ministers. Once feeling counts as proof, the old guard's rules stop working, and the church divides.

speaker: maya
text: Three. How far did the Great Awakening go toward causing the American Revolution?

speaker: maya
text: Argue both sides. For: colonists learned to organize and defy the established church, in a shared experience from New England to Georgia. Against: the fires burned out decades before 1776, and plenty of patriot leaders were never awakened. The graders want the weighing, not the verdict.

speaker: maya
text: One more, fast. The Awakening and the Enlightenment both challenged authority. Which one worked through the heart, and which through the head?

speaker: maya
text: The Awakening through the heart, the Enlightenment through the head.

speaker: maya
text: Check your four boxes. The colonies learned to argue with authority —

speaker: marcus
text: with the heart, and with the head.

speaker: maya
text: Next time: colonial self-government. The assemblies learned to rule themselves while London looked the other way. And a printer named Zenger who put press freedom on trial.
